sections.h2: Can a squatter take ownership of an Illinois house?
sections.html:
Only by meeting a statutory test that takes years and includes paying the property taxes. Ownership claims based on occupation come through adverse possession provisions in Article XIII of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the best known one requires claim and color of title made in good faith, seven successive years in possession and payment of all taxes legally assessed.

A person who simply moves into a vacant house and stays does not fit that pattern. Section 13-109 is written for a claimant holding under paper title, and the owner has separate remedies against anyone entering without right.

sections.h2: What do the Illinois adverse possession statutes require?
sections.html:
Three provisions cover most Illinois cases, and each rests on time in possession.

Illinois possession statutes in Article XIII of the Code of Civil Procedure
SectionPeriodWhat the text requires
13-10120 yearsNo action to recover land or entry on it unless within 20 years after the right accrued or title or possession was acquired, except as 13-102 through 13-122 provide
13-1097 yearsActual possession under claim and color of title made in good faith, plus payment of all taxes legally assessed
13-109.12 yearsPossession by a purchaser at a judicial foreclosure sale or a buyer from the mortgagee, under a court order, plus payment of taxes

Source: 735 ILCS 5/13-101, 13-109 and 13-109.1.

Under section 13-109, a person who takes over the possession by purchase, legacy or descent before the seven years run can add that time to the earlier occupant's, so long as possession and tax payments continue. The foreclosure provision applies to actions filed 180 days or more after August 23, 2018.

sections.h2: What changes for Illinois heirs on January 1, 2027?
sections.html:
A new section, 13-109.2, created by Public Act 104-506, takes effect January 1, 2027. It lets a co-owner who inherited through intestate succession and lives in the property ask a court to be adjudged the sole owner against non-claiming relatives, if the court finds several things.

  • Each person bringing the action has household income under 80% of the area median income set by HUD for that county
  • They searched with due diligence for anyone else holding an interest
  • For 7 successive years they held exclusive possession, paid all taxes and acquired their interest through intestacy
  • For those 7 years no other tenant in common paid taxes, helped with care or upkeep, or asserted any interest

At least 2 years before suing, the claimant must record a signed declaration with the recorder of deeds and send notice to other owners by certified and first class mail, by email and text where known, and by one newspaper publication. Any owner can object by filing a signed objection with the recorder. Heirs who share an Illinois home can ask a title company how an unresolved co-owner affects a closing, and can ask the county recorder whether any declaration or objection has been filed against the parcel.

sections.h2: How can an Illinois owner remove someone who has no right to be there?
sections.html:
Illinois uses the eviction article of the Code of Civil Procedure and its criminal trespass laws. Section 9-102 lets the person entitled to possession be restored to it when a forcible entry is made, and when entry is made into vacant or unoccupied land or tenements without right or title. It also states that nothing in the article prevents law enforcement from enforcing criminal trespass under section 21-3 or from removing people or property when there is a criminal trespass.

The civil path starts in the circuit court of the county where the property sits. Under section 9-106, the owner files a complaint describing the premises and naming the defendant, and the clerk issues a summons. A complaint may not name a minor as a defendant; if it does, the whole case is dismissed and sealed. In the case, the defendant can raise any defense under a general denial, but matters not germane to possession are kept out, and a claim for rent may be joined in the complaint. When the occupant cannot be served, section 9-107 allows an affidavit and notice by posting and mailing, or by publication and mailing. The sheriff posts 3 copies of the notice in public places near the courthouse at least 10 days before the appearance date.

sections.h2: Is it a crime to stay in an Illinois house without permission?
sections.html:
It can be. Section 21-3 makes criminal trespass to real property a Class B misdemeanor when a person knowingly and without lawful authority enters or remains in a building, enters land after notice that entry is forbidden, or stays after being told to leave. Notice can be oral or written, or a printed notice posted at the main entrance. Section 19-4 separately covers criminal trespass to a residence, defined as knowingly entering or remaining without authority in a dwelling place of another.

The trespass statute does not apply to anyone living on land at the request of the owner, or under a lease or other agreement with the owner or the owner's agent. A person with a lease or permission is a tenant or guest, and removing a tenant goes through the eviction article.

  • Written notice to leave, delivered in a way you can prove
  • Photos of the property, dated, showing the condition and any unauthorized entry
  • Tax bills, deed and insurance records showing who holds title and pays
  • A police report number if a report was made

sections.h2: How does an occupant affect selling an Illinois property?
sections.html:
Document who lives in the house before listing it. If the person claims a lease, the situation is a tenancy, and section 9-102(a)(4) covers a lessee who holds possession without right after the lease ends. If the person has no right to stay, the owner can pursue the court process above and ask an Illinois attorney about timing.

The claimant under section 13-109 must show payment of the assessed taxes for the whole period, so keep the tax bills, deed and insurance records in the owner's name. Ask the circuit clerk in your county how eviction filings proceed there, and ask the sheriff's office who carries out an eviction order. A sale can close once title is clear and the occupant has left.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in Illinois?
faqs.a: Seven successive years under claim and color of title made in good faith with all taxes paid, under 735 ILCS 5/13-109. A 20 year limit applies to actions to recover land under section 13-101, and a 2 year period applies to certain judicial foreclosure purchasers under 13-109.1.

faqs.q: Does a squatter have to pay property taxes to claim a house in Illinois?
faqs.a: Yes, under section 13-109 the possessor must pay all taxes legally assessed on the land for the full period. The same requirement appears in 13-109.1 and 13-109.2.

A section effective January 1, 2027 that lets an heir who inherited as a tenant in common, lives in the home and meets an income test of under 80% of area median income ask a court for sole ownership after 7 years of exclusive possession and tax payment, with notice and a recorded declaration.

faqs.q: Can I remove an Illinois squatter myself?
faqs.a: Illinois provides a circuit court eviction action under Article IX and criminal trespass statutes enforced by law enforcement, and section 9-102 states that police may enforce criminal trespass. Ask an Illinois attorney or the circuit clerk before changing locks or removing belongings.

faqs.q: What if the occupant cannot be found to serve papers?
faqs.a: Section 9-107 allows constructive service on an unknown occupant by posting and mailing notices, or by publication and mailing, after the plaintiff files an affidavit that service could not be made. In that case the court may rule only on the eviction portion of the complaint.
